transcript:
00:00 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I see Maya, Liam, Priya, thanks for carving out time. Real quick agenda — we want to show a live onramp with our hosted gen API, demonstrate streaming behavior, go over common params and a retry playbook. Also leave time for your stack questions.
00:12 Maya Chen: Thanks Jordan. We're mostly focused on real-time summaries inside our clinician dashboard so latency is big. We'll also need to keep PHI considerations in mind — encryption at rest, SOC 2, that sort of thing.
00:25 Jordan Lee: Totally, we'll touch on SOC 2 and VPC options and then hand to Samira for the demo.
00:30 Samira Patel: Hi all. I'll start by firing a small example from the console + curl then step through streaming, parameters, and what happens if tokens time out or stream disconnects. Please interrupt any time.
00:48 Samira Patel: (screen share) Opening the Playground -> selecting a text-gen model -> I'm going to set max_tokens to 120, temperature 0.2, top_p 0.95. Note that in hosted mode we stream partial tokens as they're generated so you get low first-byte latency.
01:10 Priya Narayan: Quick q — how does the streaming chunk size work? Will we get many tiny packets that cause UI thrashing?
01:18 Samira Patel: Good call. We batch tokens at the runtime layer and normally emit chunks aligned with decoder steps; default chunking is configurable. For most UIs we recommend a 150-300ms aggregation on the client so you don't re-render per token. On our side we also have continuous batching to keep throughput efficient.
01:35 Liam Ortiz: Do you do prefix caching or KV cache reuse across sessions? We have repetitive clinical templates.
01:42 Samira Patel: Yes, we support prefix/KV caching. If you frequently send a long prompt header (like the patient instructions), we can cache those KV entries so subsequent calls skip recompute. That saves both latency and token costs. You'll want to pin model variant to ensure cache compatibility.
02:05 Jordan Lee: Quick note on model pinning: if you pin to a quantized variant for cost, the cache/compatibility and the fallback chain need to be defined, which we can show in the Console.
02:20 Maya Chen: We're concerned about retries — what does your recommended retry backoff look like for streaming?
02:26 Samira Patel: The standard pattern: detect transient network error or 5xx server error, then retry with exponential backoff with jitter. For streaming we recommend idempotency via a request id and a resume token. If a stream cuts, the client can re-open and we try to fast-forward the KV cache + resume from last emitted token.
02:50 Priya Narayan: Resume token — is that exposed in the SDK response?
02:54 Samira Patel: Yes, we return a minimal resume handle in the stream metadata. It's opaque but lets the server match the cached state. Small gotcha: if you change params (e.g., temperature or system prompt) the resume won't be valid.
03:15 Liam Ortiz: How do you avoid duplicate outputs when replays occur?
03:20 Samira Patel: We attach sequence numbers and suggest the client dedupe on the last confirmed sequence id. For most web apps a simple compare-and-append is enough.
03:33 Jordan Lee: I'll show a quick curl to demonstrate an intentional transient error and the retry cycle.
03:38 Jordan Lee: curl -X POST ... (reads example) - we pass x-request-id and accept: text/event-stream. On a simulated connection drop we re-open with the same request id and resume token — server will either continue or return final corpus if expired.
04:10 Maya Chen: That simulated drop — what are practical TTLs on resume tokens?
04:14 Samira Patel: Defaults are tuned to 30s resume windows for interactive flows, longer for batch. We can extend per-customer for Dedicated or Private.
04:30 Priya Narayan: Switching to params — what's the sensible default for temperature and top_p for deterministic summarization?
04:36 Samira Patel: For summarization we recommend temperature 0.0–0.2 and top_p around 0.8–0.95, plus a max_tokens cap. Also use stop sequences to avoid trailing hallucination.
04:52 Liam Ortiz: Cost-wise are tokens counted for both prompt and completion?
04:55 Jordan Lee: Yes, both. We show token breakouts in the Console per request so you can attribute cost to prompt vs generation.
05:05 Priya Narayan: Any quick tips to reduce token usage without hurting quality?
05:08 Samira Patel: Compress prompts — use compact system prompts or embeddings-based retrieval to send only relevant context. Enable prefix caching for repeated static headers. Also choose a lower precision model or a quantized variant to reduce per-token compute cost if quality is acceptable.
05:30 Maya Chen: You mentioned fallback models earlier — can you outline a typical routing policy?
05:35 Samira Patel: Common pattern: primary is low-latency high-quality model, fallback is cheaper quantized variant or regional replica. We route by latency SLO, cost budget, and region. If primary returns 503 or experiences high tail latency, we auto-failover to fallback per route rules.
05:58 Jordan Lee: We also offer policy-based routing so you can say 'prefer cheapest under 200ms' or 'always prefer pinned model for PHI'.
06:10 Priya Narayan: How much control does the SDK give on retries? Can we fully control backoff parameters?
06:16 Samira Patel: Yes, SDK exposes retry hooks and parameters (max_attempts, base_delay_ms, max_delay_ms, jitter) and helps you attach an idempotency key. We also provide recommended defaults.
06:30 (30s of typing noise on screen)
06:40 Samira Patel: Now I'll demo a small load where we hit 50 concurrent streams and show how the console displays per-route latency and token rate. Please note we're in a shared hosted environment so absolute numbers are demo-only.
07:02 Samira Patel: (runs demo) You can see the console shows p50/p95/p99 latency and tokens/second. If a model starts to spike p99, the automatic routing can shift a portion to the fallback to protect SLOs.
07:25 Liam Ortiz: If you shift to fallback, do you get implied changes in semantics? For us medical phrasing is sensitive.
07:31 Samira Patel: Correct, fallbacks can alter wording. That's why for regulated workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private with pinned models. For hosted we can also pin and disable fallback for critical routes.
07:48 Maya Chen: Can logs and full transcripts be redacted or omitted from retention for PHI?
07:54 Jordan Lee: Yes — you can configure retention policies and integrated KMS. For hosted we offer configurable retention windows and automatic PII redaction hooks; for Private you control the storage entirely. We'll follow up with whitepaper links.
08:12 Priya Narayan: On throughput — how does batching interact with real-time constraints? We can't wait hundreds of ms to collect batch.
08:20 Samira Patel: Our runtime does continuous batching; it forms very small micro-batches for low-latency requests and larger batches when throughput is prioritized. You set batch-size / latency targets per route. It's a tradeoff: larger batches => better GPU utilization and lower cost, but higher latency.
08:44 Jordan Lee: That's where Redwood Optimize can help — it analyzes request shapes and suggests batch settings and model variants to hit cost/latency targets.
08:55 Maya Chen: Can Optimize propose quantization levels? We worry about regressions in clinical accuracy.
09:01 Samira Patel: Yes, Optimize will suggest quantization and run a small eval using your provided prompt set and compare rouge/bleu/semantic similarity metrics — we surface the regression risk. You always get to approve a profile before rollout.
09:20 Liam Ortiz: Let's talk retries in more detail — do you recommend client-side or server-side retry orchestration?
09:27 Samira Patel: A hybrid approach: client-side retry for transient network issues; server-side orchestrated fallback for capacity-related failover. For example, if a request times out due to network drop, client retries with backoff using same request id. If server-side detects capacity issues, it can proactively route to fallback.
09:48 Priya Narayan: Anything special for idempotency on longer-running generations?
09:52 Samira Patel: Include an idempotency key and, if possible, start the request in 'generate and persist' mode where server stores checkpoint states. For very long generations we provide checkpoints so clients can resume without redoing full compute.
10:10 (short interruption, background voice)
10:18 Jordan Lee: Quick Q from Maya — how do we measure the cost impact of retries?
10:23 Samira Patel: Retries do consume compute for attempts that run. We recommend: 1) dedupe at client so you don't double-submit; 2) server-side short-circuit if duplicate idempotency key is seen; and 3) observe retry volume in Console to tune timeouts. We'll show the toggle for dedupe behavior.
10:50 Maya Chen: Could you show an example of a retry backoff header in the response?
10:55 Samira Patel: Sure. In the SDK we expose x-retry-after-ms and a small JSON block with suggested backoff and whether resume is available. If resume isn't available we include a reason.
11:10 Priya Narayan: Are resumable streams supported in mobile clients with flaky networks?
11:14 Samira Patel: Yes — we built resumed streams with small resume tokens specifically for flaky mobile networks. The client resumes with the last confirmed seq id and we attempt to continue. If the model context was evicted from cache, server returns a replay flag and you re-send prompt or use a cheaper fallback.
11:36 Jordan Lee: Let's pivot — I'll demo a quick SDK snippet showing idempotency and resume headers. (screen) code: client.generate({ idempotencyKey: 'abc123', stream: true, onResume: ... })
12:05 Maya Chen: In-situ testing — how quickly can we run a pilot? We want to test with 500 daily clinical summaries and see latency under load.
12:12 Jordan Lee: We can get you a 2-week pilot with reserved dev tokens and a small dedicated capacity window for benchmarking. Samira will run a micro-benchmark and you provide prompts.
12:24 Liam Ortiz: For compliance we will need SOC2 and architecture diagram before starting — can you send those?
12:29 Jordan Lee: Absolutely — I'll attach SOC2 summary, network diagram, and KMS/HSM docs. We'll schedule the security meeting separately.
12:40 Priya Narayan: One more — how do you surface hallucination regressions? We need monitoring.
12:45 Samira Patel: We have evaluation hooks in the Console: run prompt-based evals, compute semantic similarity vs ground truth, and set regression alerts. Optimize can also watch a small prompt set and trigger rollback if quality drops for a new model profile.
13:10 Maya Chen: Nice.
13:18 Samira Patel: Wrapping up demo — key takeaways: stream resume tokens, idempotency keys, client dedupe, and use Optimize to pick batching/model profiles.
13:34 Jordan Lee: Let's summarize next steps — I'll send starter repo + pricing, Samira will share benchmark script and run the 48-hour test, and Priya will send the prompt set. Security follow-up with Liam.
13:50 Maya Chen: Sounds good. Anything else on cost? Do you have a per-token estimate for the demo if we assume 120 tokens per summary?
13:58 Jordan Lee: Rough rule — compute cost varies by model; for a mid-range quantized model estimate you can ballpark $0.002–0.006 per 1k tokens but we'll send exact numbers in the pricing doc. The Console also shows estimate per-route.
14:20 Liam Ortiz: OK thank you. We'll review docs and pick a week for the security call.
14:27 Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes.
14:32 (call ends)

Notes on imperfections and misc: the transcript includes a couple of mis-heard acronyms (we said 'KV cache' sometimes 'K V cache' in audio), occasional filler words, and brief cross-talk.

Recap: primary deliverables: pricing + quickstart repo (Jordan); benchmark script + initial latency/cost output (Samira); prompt set and success criteria (Priya). Security deep-dive scheduled separately.
